facts.text: It has come and gone for 4 years.
It's on my trunk, arms and legs, the same on both sides, in places that don't get sun.
Over several months each patch slowly spreads outward in rings, with scaling.
When the rash flares up, my joints ache.
I take a proton pump inhibitor.
The proton pump inhibitor is the only medicine I take.
I've been treated for the rash with steroid creams and with steroids for the whole body.

facts.item: steroid treatment for the rash: response
facts.text: They only helped for a while.

findings.name: skin examination
findings.result: Pink-red, symmetric, concentric annular patches with trailing scale involving 10% to 15% of the body surface area.

findings.name: skin biopsy from the leading edge of a lesion
findings.result: Punch and broad shave biopsies: superficial perivascular and lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate with exocytosis of small lymphocytes with mild nuclear contour irregularities, minimal spongiosis, vacuolar alteration at the dermoepidermal junction and papillary dermal fibrosis; no perivascular cuffing, interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate or significant red blood cell extravasation. Immunohistochemistry: predominantly CD3+ infiltrate with an approximately equal ratio of CD4+ to CD8+ cells; loss of CD7 on lymphocytes estimated at approximately 40%. Periodic acid–Schiff diastase stain negative for fungi.

aliases: mycosis fungoides type cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
gold.reasoning: 1. Erythema gyratum repens was considered clinically because of the multiple concentric, almost targetoid rings — “presenting similarly to that of gyratum repens.” 2. Tinea corporis was excluded by negative fungal staining — “Periodic acid–Schiff diastase staining was negative for fungi.” 3. Mycosis fungoides was suspected based on lichenoid and epidermotropic lymphocytic infiltrates — “we observed some of these features, including epidermotropism, in our patient that raised the suspicion for MF despite clinical features that were unusual for this diagnosis.”
